title: Making abortable algorithms easier
body:
Warning: half-baked idea ahead.

[Conditional abort](https://infra.spec.whatwg.org/#algorithm-conditional-abort) is great, although it's somewhat awkward in larger algorithms.

Imagine:

1. Let a be the result of starting machine A.
1. Let b be the result of starting machine B.
1. Increment global counter by 1.
1. Let c be the result of starting machine C.
1. Resolve promise.

You either end up with:

1. Let a be null.
1. Let b be null.
1. Let c be null.
1. Run these steps, but abort when the user clicks the "Cancel" button:
    1. Set a to the result of starting machine A.
1. If aborted, then:
    1. Stop a.
    1. Reject promise.
    1. Abort these steps.
1. Run these steps, but abort when the user clicks the "Cancel" button:
    1. Set b to the result of starting machine B.
1. If aborted, then:
    1. Stop a.
    1. Stop b.
    1. Reject promise.
    1. Abort these steps.
1. Run these steps, but abort when the user clicks the "Cancel" button:
    1. Increment global counter by 1.
1. If aborted, then:
    1. Stop a.
    1. Stop b.
    1. Decrement global counter by 1.
    1. Reject promise.
    1. Abort these steps.
1. Run these steps, but abort when the user clicks the "Cancel" button:
    1. Set c to the result of starting machine C.
1. If aborted, then:
    1. Stop a.
    1. Stop b.
    1. Stop c.
    1. Decrement global counter by 1.
    1. Reject promise.
    1. Abort these steps.
1. Resolve promise.

Or:

1. Let a be null.
1. Let b be null.
1. Let c be null.
1. Let incremented be false.
1. Run these steps, but abort when the user clicks the "Cancel" button:
    1. Set a to the result of starting machine A.
    1. Set b to the result of starting machine B.
    1. Set c to the result of starting machine C.
    1. Increment global counter by 1 and set incremented to true.
    1. Set c to the result of starting machine C.
1. If aborted, then:
    1. If a is not null, then stop a.
    1. If b is not null, then stop b.
    1. If c is not null, then stop c.
    1. If incremented is true, then decrement global counter by 1.
    1. Reject promise.
    1. Abort these steps.
1. Resolve promise.

Instead, could we assign a 'rollback' step to particular steps? Rollback steps would be processed in reverse order, from the point the algorithm reached when it was aborted.

1. Run these steps, but cancel if the user clicks the "Cancel" button:
    
    Cancel step: Reject promise.

    1. Let a be the result of starting machine A.

        Cancel step: Stop a.

    1. Let b be the result of starting machine B.

        Cancel step: Stop b.

    1. Increment global counter by 1.

        Cancel step: Decrement global counter by 1.

    1. Let c be the result of starting machine C.

        Cancel step: Stop c.

    1. Resolve promise.
